Designing a Food Delivery Service Like Zomato / Uber Eats / DoorDash

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate–Advanced Prerequisites:Geospatial Indexing, Message Queues, and WebSockets

TL;DR

A food delivery platform connects customers, restaurants, and riders. The system handles search (Elasticsearch), ordering (Postgres), live rider tracking (Redis Geo + WebSocket), and dispatch matching (Temporal workflow).

💡 Elasticsearch is a search engine optimized for full-text search, filtering, and faceted queries. It indexes data in inverted indexes for sub-100ms search across millions of documents.

New components:

  • Search (Elasticsearch): Answers “biryani near me, pure veg, 4+ stars” in one query. It exists because the catalog question is text plus location plus filters, which a plain SQL WHERE cannot rank.
  • Order Service: Owns the order’s lifecycle and its money. Separate from search because it needs transactional correctness, not throughput.
  • Location (Redis Geo): Holds every rider’s current coordinates in memory. It exists because 200K riders pinging every few seconds is too much write traffic for the orders database.
  • Dispatch (Temporal): Runs the multi-step “offer to a rider, wait, try the next one” process. It exists because that process has to survive a server restart halfway through.
  • WebSocket gateway: Keeps one open connection per watching customer so rider positions can be pushed, not polled.

In 3 sentences: Customer searches for restaurants (Elasticsearch with geo + relevance scoring), places an order (Postgres with idempotency), and the system finds a nearby rider (Redis Geo for proximity, Temporal for the multi-step dispatch workflow). The rider’s live location streams to the customer via WebSocket. Each component is independently scalable.

💡 WebSocket is a persistent two-way connection. Unlike HTTP (ask → answer → done), WebSocket stays open so the server can push updates instantly. Learn more →

Understanding the Problem

🍔 What is Zomato? Zomato (known as Uber Eats or DoorDash in the US) is an on-demand food delivery platform that connects customers with nearby restaurants. Customers browse menus, place orders, pay, and watch their food travel from the restaurant to their door via a delivery partner.

Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • DoorDash Dispatch - Builds assignment algorithms that balance delivery time, driver earnings, and restaurant readiness. Uses machine learning (ML) models for estimated time of arrival (ETA) prediction and dynamic batching. (DoorDash Engineering)
  • Uber Eats Marketplace - Three-sided marketplace (eaters, restaurants, couriers) with real-time dispatch using geospatial indexing. Open-sourced Cadence for workflow orchestration. (Uber Engineering)
  • Swiggy Search - Elasticsearch-based restaurant discovery with personalized ranking, geolocation filtering, and real-time availability. Handles 50K+ queries per second (QPS) during peak hours. (Swiggy Engineering)
  • Grab GrabNearby - Redis Geo for sub-10ms rider proximity queries across Southeast Asia. Location time to live (TTL) ensures stale drivers auto-expire. (Grab Engineering)💡 A TTL is an expiry stamp attached to a stored value. When it elapses the store deletes the value itself, so a rider who stops reporting disappears from the “available now” set with no cleanup job.

Functional Requirements

Core Requirements

  1. Customers should be able to search for nearby restaurants and browse their menus.
  2. Customers should be able to place an order and pay for it.
  3. The system should dispatch the order to an available delivery partner and let the customer track it in real time.

Below the line (out of scope)

  • Ratings and reviews for restaurants and riders
  • Promotions, coupons, loyalty programs
  • Scheduled / group orders
  • Restaurant onboarding and menu management tooling
  • Multi-restaurant carts

Non-Functional Requirements

Core Requirements

  • Low latency for search and order placement: search < 300 ms P95 (the latency 95% of requests beat), order placement < 1 s P95.
  • Strong consistency for order state and payment - no double charges, no two riders assigned to one order.💡 Strong consistency means every reader sees the latest write immediately. It matters here because an order’s status and a rider’s assignment are facts two services must never disagree about.
  • High throughput at peak - dinner rush in a metro can generate 100K+ orders/hour and 200K+ live rider GPS streams.
  • Real-time tracking - rider location visible to the customer within 2 seconds of each update.

Below the line

  • Fine-grained access control, General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) / Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) compliance💡 GDPR in Europe and DPDP in India are data-protection laws. They constrain which personal fields you may keep and for how long, which in this design mostly bites on the rider location trail.
  • Disaster recovery with multi-region failover
  • Continuous integration / continuous deployment (CI/CD) and zero-downtime deploys
  • Full observability stack

Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Users: 20M daily active users (DAU), 200K peak concurrent💡 Back-of-envelope estimation is rough arithmetic done before any design choice, so that each component is picked against a number rather than a feeling. Learn more →
  • Write QPS: ~50K rider location writes/sec (200K active riders × 1 ping every 4s during peak)
  • Read QPS: 20M DAU × ~10 searches/day ≈ 200M searches/day, which averages only ~2.3K/sec – but food delivery is savagely peaked around lunch and dinner. Assume 50K QPS at the worst minute and design for that.
  • Storage: ~500GB orders DB/year (100K orders/hour peak × order metadata)
  • Bandwidth: ~2 gigabits per second (Gbps) at peak (search responses + tracking WebSocket streams)

Core Entities

  • Customer - user placing the order.
  • Restaurant - merchant with a menu and operating hours.
  • Menu Item - a dish belonging to a restaurant, with price and availability.
  • Order - a confirmed request linking a customer, a restaurant, and items, with lifecycle state.
  • Delivery Partner (Rider) - the person physically delivering the order; has a live location.
  • Payment - the financial transaction tied to an order.

API / System Interface

GET  /v1/restaurants?lat=<>&lng=<>&q=<>        → Restaurant[]
GET  /v1/restaurants/:id/menu                  → Menu
POST /v1/orders                                → Order
     Body: { restaurantId, items, addressId, paymentMethod }
     Header: Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
POST /v1/riders/location                       → 200
     Body: { lat, lng }
     (riderId comes from JWT, never trust the body)
PATCH /v1/rides/:rideId                        → Ride
     Body: { accept | decline }
GET  /v1/orders/:id/track                      → WebSocket stream

Security: every endpoint requires a JSON Web Token (JWT). customerId, riderId, and server-side amounts must never be taken from the client body.💡 A JWT is a small signed token the client presents on every request. Because the server verifies the signature it can trust the user id inside it, which is why the id never needs to come from the request body where a user could edit it. Learn more →

High-Level Design

Let’s build up the design by walking through each functional requirement.

1) Customers can search restaurants and browse menus

Customer opens the app → hits our backend through an API Gateway → a Restaurant Service returns a list of nearby restaurants filtered by location, cuisine, and availability.

New components we need:

  1. API Gateway - authenticates users, applies rate limits, and routes to the right service. Every request passes through here first.
  2. Restaurant Service - handles restaurant listings and menus. Reads from the database and returns results filtered by location and availability.
  3. Restaurants and Menus DB - stores restaurant info, operating hours, and menu items. The source of truth for catalog data.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Customer opens the app and types “biryani” → app calls GET /v1/restaurants?lat=12.9&lng=77.6&q=biryani
  2. API Gateway checks: valid JWT? Within rate limits? Good → forwards to Restaurant Service
  3. Restaurant Service queries the database for restaurants near the customer’s coordinates that serve biryani and are currently open
  4. Customer picks “Hyderabad House” and taps it → app calls GET /v1/restaurants/:id/menu → same service returns the full menu with prices and availability

What FR1 leaves broken: this is a WHERE name ILIKE '%biryani%' over 500K restaurants, and it is the wrong tool in four separate ways. It cannot rank by relevance, so results come back in whatever order the planner felt like. It has no typo tolerance, so “biriyani” returns an empty screen. Every facet count (“how many pure veg? how many 4-star?”) is its own COUNT(*) GROUP BY. And it runs on the same Postgres that will own orders and payments, so search traffic competes with checkout. It holds up to roughly 50 QPS and the requirement is three orders of magnitude past that. Deep Dive 5 earns a real search tier.

2) Customers can place and pay for an order

When the customer confirms a cart, we need to create an order, charge them, and move on to dispatch. We add an Order Service and a Payment Service.

New components we need (in addition to the ones above):

  1. Order Service - the order lifecycle manager. Creates orders, validates carts, computes totals, and manages the order state machine from CREATED → DELIVERED.💡 This service is the single source of truth for “what’s happening with my order?” - every state change goes through it.
  2. Payment Service - handles charging the customer. Wraps the payment gateway and manages the authorization + capture flow.
  3. Orders DB (Postgres) - stores order state with strong consistency. We use Postgres because money is involved - atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability (ACID) transactions prevent double-charges and lost orders.💡 An ACID transaction groups several writes so they all land or none of them do, and so a half-finished transaction is never visible to anyone else. Here it keeps the order row and the payment row from ever disagreeing.
  4. Payment Gateway (Razorpay, Stripe, Unified Payments Interface or UPI) - the external service that actually moves money. We don’t process cards ourselves - that would require Payment Card Industry (PCI) compliance.💡 The gateway is a “trusted intermediary” between us and banks.💡 PCI DSS is the card-industry security standard you must be audited against if your own servers ever touch raw card numbers. Handing the card to a gateway means the audit is their problem, not ours.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Customer confirms their cart → app calls POST /v1/orders with an Idempotency-Key (so accidental retries don’t create double orders)
  2. Order Service validates: Are all items still available? Is the restaurant still open? It computes the authoritative total itself - never trust the client’s amount (clients can be tampered with)
  3. Order Service calls Payment Service → which authorizes the charge through Razorpay/Stripe/UPI
  4. On payment success → Order Service writes the order with status CONFIRMED to Postgres (one atomic transaction: order + payment record)
  5. Customer sees “Order Confirmed! 🎉” - now the dispatch flow kicks in

Why the idempotency key? Indian mobile networks are flaky. The user’s phone might retry the request when it loses signal for a second. Without an idempotency key, they’d get charged twice. With it, the second request returns the same response as the first - safe retries for free.

What FR2 leaves broken: the idempotency key covers the customer retrying, which is the common case. It does not cover us retrying. The call to Razorpay sits synchronously inside the customer’s request, and a gateway timeout is ambiguous by construction – the money may have moved or may not have. FR2 treats a timeout as a failure and returns an error, which means a charged customer with no order. Nothing here closes that gap, and nothing in the deep dives does either: the real answer is a settlement reconciliation job against the gateway’s own ledger, and that is below the line on this page. Worth saying out loud rather than leaving the reader to assume the ACID transaction covered it. It does not – the transaction spans our two tables, not the bank.

3) Match a rider and let the customer track the delivery

Now we introduce a Rider Client, a Location Service that receives live GPS pings, and a Ride Matching Service that picks a rider for each confirmed order. We also need a push channel so the rider gets notified immediately.

New components we need (in addition to the ones above):

  1. Location Service - ingests live GPS pings from rider phones (every 3-5 seconds) and stores them. The “where is everyone right now?” service.
  2. rider_locations table in Postgres - one row per rider, overwritten on each ping, with a B-tree on (lat, lng). The simplest thing that answers “where is everyone.”💡 A B-tree is the ordinary database index: a sorted tree that turns “find this value” into a handful of hops instead of a full table read. It sorts on one dimension at a time, which is exactly why it struggles with “near this point” later on.
  3. Ride Matching Service - finds the best available rider for a confirmed order. Queries nearby riders, scores them, and sends an offer.
  4. Notification Service - pushes the ride offer to the rider’s phone via FCM/APNs. Also notifies the customer about order updates.
  5. FCM / APNs - Firebase Cloud Messaging and Apple Push Notification service. External services that deliver push notifications to rider phones, even when the app is backgrounded.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Riders’ phones stream GPS pings to the Location Service every few seconds. Location Service runs an UPDATE rider_locations SET lat=?, lng=?, updated_at=now() WHERE rider_id=? per ping
  2. Once the order hits CONFIRMED, the Order Service fires a “find me a rider” request to the Ride Matching Service
  3. Matching Service runs a bounding-box query against rider_locations: riders whose lat and lng fall within roughly 3km of Hyderabad House, who are marked available, and whose updated_at is within the last 30 seconds
  4. Matching picks the best rider (closest + high acceptance rate + estimated pickup time) and sends them an offer via the Notification Service → rider’s phone buzzes with “New delivery: Hyderabad House → 2.1km away”
  5. Rider taps “Accept” → PATCH request comes in → Order Service updates state to RIDER_ASSIGNED
  6. The customer’s app polls GET /v1/orders/:id every 3 seconds and redraws the rider’s dot wherever the last poll said it was

What FR3 leaves broken: everything expensive about this requirement is still ahead of us.

  • The write volume does not fit. 200K riders at a ping every 4 seconds is 50K UPDATEs/sec, each one a row write plus two index updates, against the same Postgres that owns orders and payments. Deep Dive 1 moves live position somewhere that can absorb it.
  • The proximity query is the wrong shape. A B-tree on (lat, lng) is two one-dimensional indexes wearing a trenchcoat – it can narrow on latitude and then has to scan every rider in that band. It does not understand 2D. Deep Dive 1 fixes that too.
  • Matching sends one offer and then stops caring. If the rider’s phone is face-down in a pocket, nothing times the offer out and nothing moves to the next candidate. The order sits in CONFIRMED indefinitely. Deep Dive 4 makes dispatch durable.
  • Nothing stops two offers colliding. Two orders from the same neighbourhood can both score the same rider top, and two riders can both accept the same order. Deep Dive 2 is about which store each of those invariants belongs in.
  • Tracking is a 3-second poll. The NFR asks for rider position within 2 seconds of each update and a poll cannot get there. Deep Dive 3 earns the push channel.

Technology Choices

Tier Purpose Primary Pick Alternatives Why Primary Wins Here
Search Index Restaurant discovery with geo + relevance Elasticsearch Algolia, Meilisearch, Typesense Geo-distance scoring + full-text + facets (cuisine, rating, delivery time) in one query
Order DB Order state machine + payment records Postgres CockroachDB, MySQL, Spanner ACID for payment consistency; order volume fits sharded Postgres
Location Store Real-time rider GPS coordinates Redis Geo PostGIS, ElastiCache, DynamoDB Sub-ms GEORADIUS queries; TTL auto-expires stale rider positions
Dispatch Workflow Multi-step rider assignment orchestration Temporal Cadence, Step Functions, custom state machine Handles timeouts, retries, and human-in-loop (rider acceptance) as durable workflow
Event Bus Order events, location streams, notifications Kafka Kinesis, Pulsar, RabbitMQ Ordered per-order-id partition; replay for failed consumers
Real-time Push Live tracking to customer app WebSocket SSE, Long Polling, gRPC stream Bi-directional for tracking + rider chat; persistent connection during order lifecycle
CDN Menu images, restaurant photos CloudFront Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai High cache-hit for static menu assets; edge compression for mobile
scroll →

Why Redis Geo over PostGIS for rider location? 200K riders pinging every 4 seconds is ~50K writes/sec. Redis Geo handles that in memory with O(log N) for GEOADD and GEORADIUS. PostGIS would require disk I/O per write and can’t match the throughput for ephemeral location data that expires in seconds.💡 PostGIS is an extension that teaches Postgres real two-dimensional geometry, so “within 3 km of this point” becomes an index lookup instead of a scan. Learn more → Deep Dive 1 works through why fixing only the read side with PostGIS is the wrong half of the problem.

Data Modeling

Postgres (Order DB — order lifecycle):

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id UUID NOT NULL,
    restaurant_id UUID NOT NULL,
    rider_id UUID,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,  -- CREATED, CONFIRMED, ASSIGNED, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED
    items JSONB NOT NULL,
    total_amount DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    delivery_address JSONB NOT NULL,
    payment_method VARCHAR(20),
    payment_status VARCHAR(15),
    idempotency_key UUID UNIQUE,
    placed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    delivered_at TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id, placed_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_restaurant ON orders(restaurant_id, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_rider ON orders(rider_id, status);

-- A rider can hold at most one in-flight order. This is the invariant that
-- stops double-booking; see Deep Dive 2.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_order_per_rider ON orders (rider_id)
WHERE status IN ('ASSIGNED', 'READY', 'PICKED_UP');
SQL

Redis Geo (Location Store — real-time rider positions):

Key: "riders:active:{city}" → Geo Set (member = riderId, lat/lng as geohash score)
Key: "rider:status:{riderId}" → Hash { status, orderId, lastPing, heading }
TTL: 30s on status key (auto-expires stale riders)

Elasticsearch (Search Index — restaurant discovery):

Index: restaurants
  Fields: name (text), cuisines (keyword[]), rating (float), delivery_time_min (int),
          price_range (int), is_open (boolean), location (geo_point), city (keyword)
  Scoring: function_score combining relevance + geo_distance + rating boost

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Search restaurants near me Elasticsearch geo_distance filter + function_score (relevance × proximity × rating)
Place order Postgres INSERT INTO orders with status=PLACED, trigger Temporal workflow
Find nearest rider Redis Geo GEOSEARCH riders:active:{city} FROMLONLAT lng lat BYRADIUS 5 km COUNT 10 ASC
Update rider location Redis Geo GEOADD riders:active:{city} lng lat riderId every 3-5s
Track order live WebSocket + Redis Pub/Sub Subscribe to ride:track:{orderId}, rider publishes location updates
scroll →

How Rider Dispatch Works (Temporal Workflow):

  1. Order confirmed → Temporal starts a dispatch_workflow with 5-minute timeout💡 Temporal is a service that runs long multi-step processes reliably: it records the outcome of each step, so if the machine running the process dies another one resumes from the last recorded step instead of starting over. Deep Dive 4 explains why dispatch needs that. Learn more →
  2. Workflow calls GEOSEARCH riders:active:{city} to find 5 nearest available riders
  3. Sends ride offer to top candidate via WebSocket. Starts 30s accept timer.
  4. If accepted: assign rider to order, update Postgres, publish event. Workflow completes.
  5. If declined/timeout: try next candidate. After 5 candidates or 5 minutes: escalate (expand radius, boost payout)
  6. Temporal handles crash recovery: if worker dies mid-dispatch, another picks up from the last checkpoint

Deep Dives

Deep Dive 1 - How do we handle 200K riders pinging their location every few seconds?

In simple terms: 200K delivery drivers are sending their GPS location every 4 seconds. That’s 50K writes per second of tiny geo records. A normal database can’t handle this volume.

Problem. 200K riders × 1 ping / 4s ≈ 50K writes/sec of tiny geo records. Standard databases (PostgreSQL, DynamoDB) would either fall over on write volume or cost a fortune. And we also need to answer “give me riders within 3 km of this point” fast - a lat/lng scan of millions of rows is a non-starter.

Bad - the rider_locations table FR3 built: Postgres, a row per rider, a B-tree on (lat, lng). Two problems, and the read one is the subtler of the two. A B-tree over (lat, lng) is a one-dimensional structure pretending to be two: it can seek to the right latitude band and then has to scan every rider in that band to filter on longitude. In a dense city that band is most of your fleet, so the “within 3km” query degrades toward a scan of the city – and it runs on every single order, 100K+ per hour at dinner. On the write side, 50K UPDATEs/sec against an indexed table means 50K row writes plus index maintenance plus write-ahead log (WAL) traffic, on the same cluster that commits payments. The write amplification is the part that bites first.

Two problems, and the read one is the subtler of the two. A B-tree over is a one-dimensional structure pretending to be two: it can seek to the right latitude band and then has to scan every rider in that band to filter on longitude. In a dense city that band is most of your fleet, so the “within 3km” query degrades toward a scan of the city – and it runs on every single order, 100K+ per hour at dinner. On the write side, 50K s/sec against an indexed table means 50K row writes plus index maintenance plus traffic, on the same cluster that commits payments. The write amplification is the part that bites first.

PostGIS adds R-tree / GiST indexes tuned for 2D queries. gives you nearby riders in log N. That genuinely fixes the read side – the query now understands two dimensions. But the writes are unchanged: 50K/sec still land on disk, each costing multiple disk input/output operations (IOs), and a GiST index is expensive to maintain than the B-tree you replaced. You have fixed the half of the problem that was cheaper to fix.

Redis Geo (backed by sorted sets under the hood with geohash scoring) stores rider positions entirely in memory:

by keeps each Redis shard small (say 10K riders) and evenly distributed. Riders don’t cross city boundaries often.

Freshness over durability is the right tradeoff here - if Redis loses a few seconds of pings, the rider just shows up again on the next ping. We still tee every ping to Kafka for a durable history stream consumed by analytics and fraud detection, not by the matching hot path.

💡

Client-side optimization matters too. Instead of dumb 5s intervals, the rider app can adapt:

If roughly a third of the fleet is idle at any moment, that trims total ping volume by about a quarter at peak, and much more off-peak when most riders are parked.

Deep Dive 2 - How do we make sure one rider isn’t offered the same order twice, and one order isn’t offered to two riders at the same time?

Problem. Matching is a race, and it’s really two races that need two different answers:

  • One order → one rider. Two riders must not both end up assigned to the same order.
  • One rider → one order. Multiple concurrent orders in the same area may see the same candidate rider at the top of their list, and must not double-book them.

These look like the same problem but they guard different rows, so a single mechanism won’t cover both. Getting this distinction wrong is the most common mistake here.

In simple terms: One order might get accepted by two drivers - that needs a conditional write on the order row. Separately, two orders in the same area might both grab the driver they each scored as the ‘best match’ - that needs a lock on the driver. Same-looking bug, two different fixes.

Bad - what FR3 does: score the candidates, offer to the top one, write the assignment on accept. At 100K+ orders/hour a metro places ~28 orders a second, and they are not spread evenly – dense restaurant clusters mean two orders placed in the same second often query nearly the same 3km circle and get back nearly the same ranked list. The top candidate is the same rider. Both offers go out, both riders see an offer, and whichever accepts second overwrites the first assignment with a plain UPDATE orders SET rider_id = .... Nobody is told. A rider rides to a restaurant for an order that is no longer theirs, and the customer whose order got silently reassigned watches a dot that isn’t coming.

The top candidate is the same rider. Both offers go out, both riders see an offer, and whichever accepts second overwrites the first assignment with a plain . Nobody is told. A rider rides to a restaurant for an order that is no longer theirs, and the customer whose order got silently reassigned watches a dot that isn’t coming.

Before sending an offer, try .

This is the same “reserve a ticket at checkout” pattern from Ticketmaster. But notice what the key is: the . This lock stops one rider from holding two live offers. It says nothing at all about the order.

The order-side race belongs in Postgres, which is the source of truth for the assignment. On accept, the Order Service runs a conditional update:



💡 Two simultaneous accepts serialize on the row lock. One updates 1 row and wins; the other gets 0 rows back and learns the order is already taken. , not the Redis lock, is what makes “one order → one rider” correct.


The rider-side race needs its own guard, because the CAS above structurally cannot see it: order A and order B are , so both pass that clause and both happily assign the same rider. Enforce it where the uniqueness actually lives:




The second writer violates the constraint and rolls back.


So what is the Redis lock for? It’s an optimization, not the correctness boundary - it stops us burning offers on a rider who already has one pending, and it gives us a cheap 10-second accept window without touching Postgres on every candidate. Keep it, but don’t lean on it for correctness.


One more case it does handle well: a rider taps accept after the TTL lapsed and someone else took the slot. Store the offer id as the lock value (), have the accept request carry it, and run a Lua compare-and-delete that honors the accept only if the value still matches. Late accepts are rejected cleanly.


💡 




Deep Dive 3 - A rider moves every four seconds. How does that reach the customer’s map in under two?


Problem. The customer’s map needs to show the rider moving smoothly. We can’t have the app hammer the server with polling queries - at 20 million DAU, that’s catastrophic.


In simple terms: The customer wants to see their delivery driver moving on the map in real-time. Polling the server every 2 seconds for 20M users = catastrophic load. We need push updates.


Bad - the 3-second poll FR3 built.
At 100K+ orders/hour, an average 40-minute delivery leaves roughly 70K deliveries in flight at any moment during dinner rush. Each app polling every 3 seconds is ~23K requests/sec whose entire job is to re-read a row. It is also the wrong shape: the poll interval and the ping interval are unrelated, so a customer either sees a position up to 3 seconds stale (missing the 2-second NFR) or asks more often than the rider reports and burns requests on identical answers. The dot also jumps between sampled points instead of moving, because polling samples a position rather than receiving a stream.

Each app polling every 3 seconds is ~23K requests/sec whose entire job is to re-read a row. It is also the wrong : the poll interval and the ping interval are unrelated, so a customer either sees a position up to 3 seconds stale (missing the 2-second NFR) or asks more often than the rider reports and burns requests on identical answers. The dot also jumps between sampled points instead of moving, because polling samples a position rather than receiving a stream.



SSE gives one-way server → client push over a long-lived HTTP connection. Works well for pure read streams like live tracking. But iOS Safari support is flaky for SSE, and you lose the persistent connection during app backgrounding.




    
 
 
 
 



 at the edge routes all subscribers for one order to the same gateway pod, keeping Pub/Sub fan-out local. Supports millions of concurrent connections with a few hundred pods.




Deep Dive 4 - What if no rider accepts? What if the gateway loses the accept?


Problem. This is a multi-step human-in-the-loop workflow. Any step can fail: rider doesn’t respond, app crashes, phone loses signal, offer times out. We need to move on to the next rider automatically and never strand an order.


In simple terms: We sent a delivery offer to a rider. They didn’t respond (phone died, went to bathroom). We need to automatically move to the next rider after a timeout without losing the order.


Bad - what FR3 actually does, which is nothing. Matching sends one offer and returns.
    
 
  • There is no timer at all. A rider whose phone is in a jacket pocket silently absorbs the order, and it stays in CONFIRMED until a human notices. Rider acceptance rates in food delivery are nowhere near 100%, so this is not an edge case – it is a large fraction of all dispatches.
    • 
 
  • The obvious patch is an in-process timer in the matching service: offer, setTimeout(10s), move to the next candidate. That moves the failure rather than removing it. Deploys roll pods several times a day, and every pod restart drops every timer it was holding – those orders hang with no record that anything was ever owed to them.
    • 

 Matching sends one offer and returns.


    
 
 




Matching state lives in a DB, a background worker looks for expired offers and triggers reassignment. Works but you’re hand-rolling a workflow engine and retry logic, which is always more subtle than it looks.



The whole matching workflow is expressed as a Temporal workflow: “offer to top rider, wait 10s, if no accept, offer to next rider, repeat up to N times, then emit DispatchFailed.” Temporal persists every step’s state to its own storage. If any worker crashes, another worker picks up the exact same workflow at the exact same step - no custom retry code needed.


Uber themselves open-sourced Cadence for exactly this reason; food-delivery dispatch is the same class of problem.




Deep Dive 5 - How do we search across 500K restaurants with text, filters, and ranking?


Problem. Zomato isn’t just “tap the nearest pin” - customers type “biryani,” filter by “pure veg, rating 4+, under ₹300,” and expect relevant results in under 300ms. At 50K search QPS peak across a catalog of 500K restaurants with nested menu items, the requirements are: text search, faceted filters, geo constraint, custom ranking, and personalization, all at low latency.


In simple terms: Customers type ‘biryani’ and expect results in under 300ms, filtered by location, rating, price, and dietary preferences. A regular SQL query can’t handle this complexity at speed.


Bad - WHERE name ILIKE '%biryani%' AND is_open = true on Postgres.
Full table scans. No relevance ranking. No typo tolerance - “biriyani” returns nothing. Facet counts (how many veg results? how many 4+ rated?) require a separate aggregation query per facet. Falls apart past 50 QPS.

Full table scans. No relevance ranking. No typo tolerance - “biriyani” returns nothing. Facet counts (how many veg results? how many 4+ rated?) require a separate aggregation query per facet. Falls apart past 50 QPS.



Adds a GIN-indexed column, handles stemming and basic relevance. Works for small catalogs. But:


    
 
 
 
 




Elasticsearch is purpose-built for exactly this workload:


    
 
 
 
 
 



Index structure - one document per restaurant with denormalized menu highlights:




A query blends relevance + distance + rating in one shot:




 Restaurants and menus live in the primary DB (Postgres or Mongo). We don’t dual-write - that leads to drift. Instead, Debezium tails the DB’s change log and publishes to a Kafka topic; a Kafka consumer materializes the search document and bulk-indexes it into Elasticsearch. End-to-end lag under 3 seconds is fine for a catalog that changes slowly.


💡 


 Popular queries ( in Bangalore CBD) repeat constantly. Cache the top results in Redis with a key like and a 60-second TTL. Use single-flight / request coalescing on cache miss so a viral query doesn’t Elasticsearch.






    
 
 
 
 
 



This is why a separate search tier matters: we get text, geo, facets, and relevance ranking in one system, decoupled from the OLTP database that owns the truth.




Core Flows


Here’s how each functional requirement plays out end-to-end across the system.


Flow 1 - Search for nearby restaurants




    
 
  1. Gateway validates the JWT and applies per-user rate limits.
    2. 
 
  2. Search Service computes a cache key from a coarse geohash plus the query and filter fingerprint.
    3. 
 
  3. Cache miss hits Elasticsearch with a function_score query blending text relevance, geo distance, rating, and popularity in one shot.
    4. 
 
  4. Results are cached for 60 seconds with request coalescing to prevent stampedes on viral queries.
    5. 
 
  5. Customer picks a restaurant; client fetches the menu directly from the Restaurant Service.
    6. 



Flow 2 - Place and pay for an order




    
 
  1. Client generates a UUIDv4 idempotency key tied to the cart. Retries reuse the same key.
    2. 
 
  2. Order Service checks Redis for the key; duplicate retries replay the cached response with no duplicate processing.
    3. 
 
  3. Server recomputes the total authoritatively - never trust a client-supplied amount.
    4. 
 
  4. Payment Service authorizes through the gateway. For UPI this is immediate; for 3-D Secure (3DS) cards the client finishes the extra step before capture.💡 UPI is India’s instant bank-to-bank payment rail: it confirms or fails in seconds with no separate capture step. 3DS is the bank’s extra “approve this on your phone” challenge for a card, which is why the card path has a second round trip the UPI path does not.
    5. 
 
  5. Order row plus outbox row go in one Postgres transaction - either both land or neither does.
    6. 
 
  6. Debezium tails the WAL and publishes OrderConfirmed to Kafka for downstream services.
    7. 



Failure worth calling out: if the gateway times out, the order stays in PAYMENT_PENDING. A reconciler polls the gateway every 5 minutes and either promotes to CONFIRMED or cancels with refund - gateway truth always wins.💡 A reconciler is a background job that compares our records against an authoritative outside source and repairs the difference. It exists because a timed-out call leaves us genuinely not knowing whether the money moved, and only the gateway can settle the question.


Flow 3a - Dispatch a rider




    
 
  1. Dispatch consumes OrderConfirmed from a Kafka topic partitioned by city_id so one worker owns each city and there’s no cross-worker race.
    2. 
 
  2. Redis Geo returns nearby riders; the ML scorer ranks them by distance, acceptance rate, and expected pickup time.
    3. 
 
  3. Before sending an offer, Dispatch grabs a per-rider lock whose value is the offer id - SET offer:rider:r1 "orderA:42" NX PX 10000. This is de-duplication of offers, not the assignment itself.
    4. 
 
  4. Rider taps accept; the request carries the offer id. A Lua compare-and-delete verifies it still matches. Mismatch means the offer expired and someone else owns the slot - clean rejection.
    5. 
 
  5. The assignment is only real once Order Service lands the CAS (... WHERE status = 'CONFIRMED' AND rider_id IS NULL). If two accepts somehow reach it, the loser gets 0 rows and is told the order is taken.
    6. 
 
  6. On timeout or reject, Dispatch picks the next candidate. After N unsuccessful rounds, escalate to ops or cancel with refund.
    7. 



Flow 3b - Live tracking




    
 
  1. Rider app streams GPS pings over a long-lived gRPC connection.💡 gRPC can hold one connection open and push many small messages down it, which is far cheaper per ping than opening a fresh HTTP request every four seconds. Intervals are adaptive - 30s when stationary, 3-5s moving, immediate on sharp turns - which trims roughly a quarter of peak ping volume and much more off-peak.
    2. 
 
  2. Location Service validates each ping, updates Redis Geo for the matching hot path, publishes to a Redis Pub/Sub channel for customer fan-out, and tees a copy to Kafka for history.
    3. 
 
  3. Customer opens tracking; WebSocket connects and subscribes to the order’s channel.
    4. 
 
  4. Consistent hashing at the edge routes all subscribers for one order to the same gateway pod, keeping Pub/Sub fan-out local.
    5. 
 
  5. Kafka feeds the durable history tier (ClickHouse warm, Simple Storage Service (S3) cold) for fraud, payouts, and ETA model training.💡 ClickHouse is a column-oriented database built for scanning and summing huge volumes of recent events. S3 is bulk file storage - far cheaper per byte, far slower to query - which is why old trails move there. Learn more →
    6. 



Order state machine


For clarity, here’s the full state progression driven by events from the flows above:




Every transition is a compare-and-set in Postgres (UPDATE ... WHERE status = expected_current), so no consumer can push the order into an illegal state. Each transition writes an outbox row that fans out via Kafka to notification, analytics, and recommendation services.




Final Architecture


Putting it all together:




New components: nothing new here - this is every piece from the deep dives on one page. Two naming notes, because the same box has picked up several labels along the way:


    
 
  • Dispatch Workflow is the component called the Ride Matching Service in FR3 and the Dispatch Service in Flow 3a. One component, three labels: the Temporal workflow that picks a rider for an order.
    • 
 
  • WebSocket (live tracking) is the gateway from Deep Dive 3. It is fed by Redis Pub/Sub on the live path; the Kafka edge into it in this diagram carries order-event notifications rather than per-ping positions.
    • 



That’s the design. Five deep dives in Bad / Good / Great progression, each picking the right primitive for the problem: Redis Geo for live rider locations, a Postgres compare-and-set plus a rider-side unique index for correct matching, WebSockets plus Pub/Sub for real-time tracking, Temporal for durable multi-step dispatch, and Elasticsearch fed by CDC for catalog search.


How it works end-to-end (order path):


    
 
  1. Customer places order — request hits API Gateway, routed to Order Service
    2. 
 
  2. Order persisted and payment charged — Order Service writes to Orders DB (Postgres), Payment Service charges via Razorpay/Stripe/UPI
    3. 
 
  3. Matching Workflow triggered — Temporal orchestrates rider assignment: queries Redis Geo for nearby riders, scores candidates, takes a per-rider offer lock, and commits the assignment with a Postgres CAS
    4. 
 
  4. Rider notified — Notification Service sends push via FCM/APNs; rider accepts or declines
    5. 
 
  5. Restaurant notified — order details sent to Restaurant App for preparation
    6. 



How it works end-to-end (live tracking path):


    
 
  1. Rider streams location — GPS pings sent to Location Service, written to Redis Geo (per city shard), events emitted to Kafka
    2. 
 
  2. Kafka sinks to history — Cassandra stores full location trail for ETA recalculation and analytics
    3. 
 
  3. Real-time push to customer — Redis PubSub routes location updates to WebSocket Gateway, customer sees rider on map
    4. 
 
  4. Search stays fresh — Debezium CDC streams restaurant DB changes to Kafka, Elasticsearch index updated in near-real-time
    5. 





Key Technologies



 
 

 Term
 What it is
 

 
 
 

 Elasticsearch
 Search engine with inverted indexes, geo-point filters, and function_score queries powering restaurant search with text + location + ranking in one call.
 

 

 Redis Geo
 In-memory geospatial index for sub-millisecond “find riders within 3km” queries on 200K+ active delivery partners.
 

 

 WebSocket
 Persistent connection streaming live rider location to customers for real-time order tracking on the map.
 

 

 Kafka
 Event bus carrying order confirmations, location streams, and CDC events between decoupled services.
 

 

 Dispatch Algorithm
 Scoring-based matching that picks the best rider using distance, acceptance rate, and estimated pickup time - not just proximity.
 

 

 Rider Assignment
 Two invariants, two mechanisms: a Postgres compare-and-set commits one rider to one order, a unique partial index on rider_id stops one rider taking two orders, and Redis SET NX de-duplicates outstanding offers.
 

 

 ETA
 Estimated Time of Arrival calculated from mapping APIs, used for rider ranking and customer-facing delivery predictions.
 

 

 CDN
 Content Delivery Network caching restaurant images and static assets at edge nodes for fast app loading.

What’s Expected at Each Level



 
This section helps you calibrate your depth. You don’t need to cover everything - just know what’s expected for your level.




Mid-level


Produce a working 3-service design (search, order, dispatch). Recognize the need for geo-queries and a basic payment flow. With prompting, discuss caching for search. You should be able to articulate why a regular SQL query won’t work for “restaurants near me” at scale, and sketch a happy-path order flow from placement to delivery.


Senior


Drive the design proactively. Propose Elasticsearch for search with CDC sync, Redis Geo for rider proximity, and idempotency for orders. Discuss real-time tracking trade-offs (polling vs WebSocket vs SSE) without prompting. You should articulate the fan-out problem for location updates and explain why the dispatch workflow needs durability beyond a simple queue.


Staff+


Address dispatch workflow durability (Temporal/Cadence), where the assignment invariants actually live (a Postgres CAS for the order, a unique partial index for the rider, and why a Redis lock alone is not the correctness boundary), adaptive location pinging to reduce write volume, and operational concerns like what happens during Redis failover. Show awareness of cost at scale - quantify rider location write volume, explain why city-sharded Redis Geo is cheaper than DynamoDB, and discuss graceful degradation when the matching service is overloaded.




🎯 Key Takeaways


    
 
  • Elasticsearch for restaurant search with geo-filtering - not a regular DB
    • 
 
  • Redis Geo for driver proximity (nearest available rider) - O(log N) queries
    • 
 
  • Kafka decouples order placement from dispatch - user doesn’t wait for driver assignment
    • 
 
  • WebSocket for live tracking - don’t poll, push
    •

Ananya Arya2mo ago
Hey I have a doubt for the ‘two riders accept the same order’ race condition, Postgres is the source of truth for rider assignment. we use an atomic conditional UPDATE that assigns the rider only if the order is still in WAITING_FOR_RIDER state and has no rider assigned. Therefore, even if two riders accept simultaneously, only one update succeeds; the other gets zero affected rows and knows the order has already been assigned.
I guess the fencing token solves a slightly different problem that 'what if a rider accepts an old offer after that offer has expired and the rider has already been offered/locked for another order?'. please correct me if i am wrong in understanding.
SystemCraftAdmin2mo ago
You've got it right. The Postgres CAS is what makes "one order → one rider" safe - row lock serializes the accepts, loser gets 0 rows. No Redis lock needed for that.

But the lock is keyed on the rider (offer:rider:{rider_id}), so it's guarding the opposite invariant: one rider not holding two live offers. A CAS on the order row can't cover that, since Order A and Order B are different rows - both pass the predicate, both commit, rider double-booked. That needs a rider-side constraint, like a unique partial index on rider_id while active.

Also, my wording was loose: that's not really a fencing token. A real one is monotonic and enforced by the resource being written to. This is a compare-and-delete on the lock value, checked in Redis. It does reject a late accept from the rider's app, which is the case you named. It wouldn't stop a stalled Dispatch worker writing to Postgres - the CAS catches that.

Rewriting the section to separate the two invariants. Good catch.
